title: The basin and towel (John 13:1–15)
hookLine: at the last supper he kneels and washes their feet
carry: as I have done to you
last: SHE HAS DONE A BEAUTIFUL THING.

lines: HE LOVED THEM UNTO THE END.
cards: Sandals, dusty roads, animals in the streets. When guests came in from the road, water was brought for their feet.
In the scriptures, washing someone else's feet is a servant's work: when David sends for Abigail, she answers that she will wash the feet of his servants.
The night before he dies, Jesus is at supper with his closest friends, and John says he knows his hour has come.
John opens the scene, in the Douay-Rheims: "having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them unto the end." To the very last. Then, in the middle of the meal, he gets up from the table.

teach.h: HE RISES, TIES ON A TOWEL.
teach.b: John slows down and gives every movement. He rises from supper. He lays aside his outer garments and ties a towel around his waist.
He pours water into a basin. He begins to wash the disciples' feet and dry them with the towel. The teacher is on his knees, doing the servant's job, friend by friend.
Judas, who will betray him, is at that table, John has told us.

teach.h: PETER: NEVER. THEN, ALL OF ME.
teach.b: Then he comes to Peter, and Peter can't bear it. Lord, are you going to wash my feet? Jesus says: you don't understand now, but you will.
Peter: "Thou shalt never wash my feet." Jesus: "If I wash thee not, thou shalt have no part with me." Then Peter swings the other way: then not only my feet, Lord, but my hands and my head.
Afterward he dresses again, sits down, and asks: do you know what I have done to you? You call me Teacher and Lord, and you're right. If I've washed your feet, you ought to wash one another's.
"For I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you do also."
Catholics relive this on Holy Thursday, at the Mass of the Lord's Supper.

teach.h: AS I HAVE DONE TO YOU, SO YOU DO ALSO.
teach.b: Where the rite is kept, the priest sets aside his outer vestment, kneels, and washes the feet of people from the parish.
The rite's old Latin name is the Mandatum, from Jesus's new commandment later that night, and it gives English the name Maundy Thursday.

how: At the Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday, the priest washes the feet of members of the congregation, a rite called the Mandatum, after the Gospel of John 13 is read.

games.q: you're Peter. your teacher is kneeling in front of you with a basin and a towel, about to wash your feet. what do you say?
games.why: “Thou shalt never wash my feet.” Jesus answers: “If I wash thee not, thou shalt have no part with me.”

practice: Think of the jobs nobody wants: cleaning the bathroom, taking out the recycling, staying late to put the chairs away, changing the diaper.
Choose one you could do for someone, unasked and unmentioned, and picture doing it slowly, with care, like the towel and the basin. If you pray, you can offer it for that person.

wordCard.voice: Mandatum. The old Latin name for Jesus washing his friends' feet and commanding them to do likewise, the root of Maundy Thursday.

orig.note: Greek: an example, a pattern to copy. What Jesus says he has given them.
